source_refs.note: 2. Swing of a Ball: a main subheading of 5.12 Uses of Bernoulli's principle, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 109-109.

blocks.text: When a ball is thrown or kicked with spin, the ball is made smoother on one side by the bowler and remains rough on the other side. The air moves faster over rough side and slows over the smoother. According to Bernoulli's equation, the faster moving air creates lower pressure, while the slower moving air creates higher pressure, this pressure difference generates a sideways force, known as Magnus effect which causes the ball to curves in the air.
book_errors: the ball is made smoother on one side by the bowler and remains rough on the other side

blocks.alt: A ball in an air stream that moves from right to left. Above the ball the streamlines crowd together (Faster air, lower pressure); below it they spread out (Slower air, higher pressure). An arrow labelled Deflection force points up from the ball. An inset labelled Spinning ball shows a small spinning ball whose path curves up away from a dashed straight line.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book captions this figure 'Turbulent flow', the caption of Fig. 5.13, but it shows air flowing past a spinning ball.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Two different effects are mixed here. The Magnus effect is caused by spin: a spinning ball drags the air round with it, so the air moves faster on one side and slower on the other, and the pressure difference curves the ball (as in Figure 5.18). A cricket ball kept shiny on one side and rough on the other swings for a different reason (the air flows differently over the rough and smooth halves); that swing is not the Magnus effect.
